one_pager.big_idea: Our brains take shortcuts that can fool us, so scientists measure, compare groups and try to prove their own ideas wrong.
goals: I can show with measurements that my perception can be wrong, and explain why scientists measure instead of trusting their eyes.
I can explain anchoring and confirmation bias using evidence from today's class tests.

flow.what: Anchoring slips handed out from the pre-shuffled pile as students arrive (Versions 1 and 2 alternate): 'Answer alone, in silence, then fold it.' Slips go into the group envelopes. Then the retrieval question: 'Hot water freezes faster than cold water': claim type and the three verdicts. Slides 1 to 2.

Muller-Lyer lines: vote A longer, B longer or the same; do not reveal and do not measure yet. Students write their prediction on the worksheet. The teacher quietly sorts the slips into Version 1 and Version 2 piles using the code in the corner. Slide 3.

Perception versus measurement; what bias means (a pull in one direction, three brain traps: eyes, numbers, looking only for 'yes'); how to measure to the nearest millimetre: start at 0, eyes directly above the mark. Do not mention anchoring yet. Slides 4 to 6.

Illusion sheets given out. Pairs predict, then measure the illusions and complete Core ('Measure, don't look!'). Two quick-finishing Recorders get the two piles of slips, the tally sheet and a calculator and work out the class means. Slide 7. If short: cut bonus illusion C (Lines E and F); teacher computes the means.

2-4-6 game from the script: groups test three numbers each round and record on the group card; the teacher answers only 'Yes' or 'No' and writes every test on the board in YES and NO columns; reveal the rule (any three numbers in increasing order) and name confirmation bias. Slides 8 to 9. If short: 3 rounds instead of 5.

Reveal the anchoring trick and the two class means; compare with the true length (about 6,300 km). 'How do scientists protect themselves from bias?': pair talk in any language, share with a frame; Stretch or Challenge if time; exit ticket and logbook line. Slides 10 to 12.

one_pager.practical: Pairs predict, then measure three optical illusions with a 30 cm ruler to the nearest mm (A and B 80 mm, C and D 20 mm, E and F 60 mm). Groups then play the 2-4-6 game, testing sets of three numbers to find a secret rule. A hidden two-version Do Now slip gives class data on anchoring.
one_pager.assessment: Exit ticket (strip at the foot of the worksheet): can the student name a bias and a protection against it, and choose the test that best checks 'add 2' (b: 1, 2, 3)? Logbook line under 'What I found': 'My brain was fooled when ___.' The bias reflection in the My thinking box is the series output for this week.
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'My eyes said ___, but the ruler showed ___.' 'The data suggests ___; however, ___.' 'This could also be explained by ___.' Chinese talk is welcome in pair talk and in the 2-4-6 group discussions; tests are called out in English numbers; the My thinking box may be in any language. Traps: 'bias' is often heard as 'unfair person', but here it is any pull in one direction, including in data; the key word table gives two Chinese terms for bias, one for results and one for people; 'estimate' is not a wild guess.
watch_out: Do not mention anchoring or the two versions before the Think phase, or the test is spoiled; say only 'Answer alone, in silence, then fold it.'
Print the illusion sheets at 100% and check A and B measure 80 mm; if the printer has scaled them, the answer key values change.

one_pager.big_idea: One result can fool us, so we repeat, calculate the mean and range, and ask whether a difference is bigger than the normal variation.
goals: I can carry out a fair ruler-drop test with five repeats per hand and calculate the mean and range.
I can write a conclusion that says whether a difference is big enough to matter, mentioning uncertainty.

flow.what: Two retrieval questions answered on the back of the worksheet: which bias in 'I only remember the days my lucky pen worked' (confirmation bias) and the mean of 12, 15, 11, 14 cm (13 cm). Slides 1 to 2.

Teacher drops the 15 cm PRIZE strip between a volunteer's finger and thumb (held at the middle); repeat with 2 or 3 volunteers; most miss. Then the claim 'Your dominant hand reacts faster than your other hand': vote Yes, No or No difference. Slides 3 to 4.

Name the variables (change which hand; measure catch distance, then reaction time; keep the same ruler, dropper, starting position, no warning); demonstrate the ruler drop with a student using the picture steps; show the conversion table and how to calculate mean and range (0.17, 0.16, 0.17, 0.15, 0.16 s: mean 0.16 s, range 0.02 s). Slides 5 to 8.

Safety slide read aloud in both languages. In pairs: 5 drops per hand per person, alternating hands, record cm and convert to seconds (partner 1 for 6 min, partner 2 for 6 min); then calculate mean and range (6 min); Stretch and Challenge. Teacher checks the 0 cm mark is level with the top of the thumb, the wait is random and hands alternate. Slides 9 to 10. If short: 3 repeats per hand, skip the Challenge formula check.

Overlap diagram: 'Is the difference big enough?' Students decide whether their own difference is bigger than their range and share with a frame; class count (dominant faster, other faster, same): 'Is that enough to give a verdict?'; exit ticket and logbook line. Slides 11 to 12. If short: class count with hands up.

one_pager.practical: Ruler-drop reaction test in pairs: the dropper holds a 30 cm ruler with the 0 cm mark level with the top of the seated catcher's thumb, waits 1 to 5 seconds and lets go without warning; the catcher reads the cm at the top of the thumb. Five drops per hand, alternating hands; each distance is converted to a time with the table, then mean and range are calculated for each hand.
one_pager.assessment: Results table with mean and range, and a conclusion that mentions uncertainty (Stretch). Spot-check 6 worksheets for correct range calculation (range errors feed into Week 5 checkpoint question 6). Exit ticket: mean (0.18 s), range (0.05 s) and one verdict (best answer: Not supported). Logbook line: 'My dominant hand was ___ by ___ s, which is / is not bigger than my range.'
hazards: Low hazard. Rulers can hit faces or fingers if flicked or swung: hold the ruler upright and still; never flick, swing or throw it.
Falling ruler near the face: keep your face away from the ruler when it drops.
Leaning or standing can lead to bumps and falls: sit down for every test.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'My dominant hand mean was ___ s and my other hand mean was ___ s.' 'The data suggests ___; however, ___.' 'To be more confident, we would need ___.' 'Our verdict is ___ because ___.' Chinese talk is welcome in pairs during the test; readings are called out in English numbers ('fourteen centimetres'). Traps: 'range' in everyday English means a choice of things, in maths it is one number (biggest minus smallest), 极差 not 范围; 'mean' is not 'means' (method); catching a ruler is a reaction, not a reflex (a reflex is automatic).
watch_out: Range errors are the most common: students write '0.15 to 0.17' instead of subtracting. Insist on one number.
Droppers who drop in a rhythm: catchers learn it and 'catch' impossibly fast (under 5 cm). Repeat those tries; the wait must be random, 1 to 5 seconds.
'A bigger distance means faster' and 'any difference in the means proves the claim': the ruler falls further when you are slower, and small differences can be normal variation.
If the ruler falls past 30 cm, write 'missed' and do that try again; a try with a slip or a warning does not count.

one_pager.big_idea: When two things change together (correlation), it does not prove that one causes the other (causation): a hidden third factor, or chance, may explain it, and graphs can be drawn to mislead.
goals: I can plot a scatter graph and describe the correlation it shows.
I can explain why a correlation does not prove causation, name a possible confounding variable, and fix a misleading graph.

flow.what: Retrieval on the back of the worksheet: reaction times 0.18, 0.15, 0.20, 0.19 s: mean (0.18 s), range (0.05 s, one number), and the three verdicts. Slides 1 to 2.
Winter graph: hot drink sales and colds both rise from October to January. 'Do hot drinks cause colds?' Vote Yes / No / Not sure and give a partner one reason; do not reveal the answer yet. Slide 3.

Positive, negative and no correlation with three mini scatter graphs (arm gestures: up, down, flat); correlation is not causation; winter as a confounding variable; three possible explanations plus chance. Slides 4 to 6.

Matching cards (4 min): pattern cards P1 to P7 to hidden-factor cards Q to W, P7 is the fair test trap; measure arm span and height (5 min), voluntary, codes not names, results on the board; plot the class scatter graph (7 min); 2 minutes slack. Sample data card for any group running late. Slides 7 to 9. If short: skip measuring and use the sample data, or cut matching to P1, P2, P4, P7.

Fix the graph (5 min): pairs answer the battery advert questions and redraw the chart from zero (Q looks 4 times taller, really 0.6 hours, about 6%); verdict: not enough evidence yet; exit ticket and logbook line (3 min). Slides 10 to 12.

one_pager.practical: Groups match 7 pattern cards to hidden-factor cards, then measure each other's height (back to the wall, book on head, sticky note) and arm span (sticky notes at the middle fingertips) to the nearest cm with a tape measure, write results on the board by code and plot the class scatter graph of arm span against height.
one_pager.assessment: Scatter graph (Core) on the worksheet and corrected bar chart on the Fix the graph sheet: collect the Fix the graph sheets to check who can explain a misleading axis. Exit ticket: confounding variable and correlation type (links to skills check question 10). Logbook line under New words: correlation, causation, confounding variable, with one example of each.
hazards: Tape measures can snap back and cut fingers or hit faces: retract slowly and keep the metal end away from faces.
Measuring bodies can feel personal: measuring is voluntary, codes not names on the board, and no comments about anyone's size.
Students who prefer not to be measured take the Measurer or Recorder role; their row uses the sample data.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'As ___ increases, ___ increases / decreases.' 'This could also be explained by ___.' 'A correlation does not prove ___ because ___.' 'The graph is misleading because ___.' Chinese talk is welcome while matching cards and discussing the graph; measurements are called out in English ('one hundred and sixty-five centimetres'). Traps: 'correlation' and 'cause' are often used as if they mean the same thing; link 'confounding' to 'confusing the picture'; the plural of 'axis' is 'axes'.
watch_out: 'If two things rise together, one must cause the other', or 'a strong correlation proves causation': even strong correlations can come from a third factor.
'A bar chart that looks very different means a big difference': always check where the axis starts.
'One odd point ruins the pattern': an anomaly should be checked, not ignored or allowed to decide the verdict.
Measuring overruns: hand the sample data card to any group running late; everyone in the class follows the same shoes rule (all on or all off).

one_pager.big_idea: To find out whether something really works, scientists run fair trials with a control group, a placebo and blinding, and they treat the people in their trials honestly and with respect.
goals: I can explain why a fair trial needs a control group, a placebo, blinding and a big enough sample.
I can compare two groups' results using means and ranges and give an honest verdict, and discuss what makes research with people ethical.

flow.what: Give out the checkpoint, read the instructions, keep time; students work alone and in silence with their own pens; collect at exactly 10 minutes and put the papers away. The incoming teacher observes. Slides 1 to 2.

Tu Youyou story: an idea from a text more than 1,600 years old, tested carefully, leading to artemisinin and a Nobel Prize. 'Should we believe an idea because it is old? How would you find out?' Slides 3 to 4.

Follow the lucky pen script exactly: a pen and a folded card for each student (alternating versions), code written on the recall sheet; study the word list for 60 seconds; count backwards in threes for 30 seconds; recall for 2 minutes with the new pen (English or Chinese); swap and mark out of 20. Slides 5 to 8.

Keep the promise straight away: reveal both cards and that every pen is identical; apologise for the trick. Teach control group, placebo, placebo effect, blind test, double-blind, random allocation and sample size. Slides 9 to 10.

Recorders call out group scores by code, never by name; class means and ranges calculated together on the board; group results table; worksheet Core and Stretch. Usual verdict: not enough evidence yet. Slide 11.

Ethics debrief with the card in pairs, any language, share with a frame, and the chance to withdraw a score with a cross on the recall sheet (5 min); exit ticket (2 min); logbook line (2 min). Use the last 2 minutes to introduce the incoming teacher. Slides 12 to 13.

one_pager.practical: Lucky pen memory trial: every student gets an identical pen and a folded card (Code 41 says it is a special 'Focus Pen', Code 52 is the control), studies 20 words for 60 seconds, counts backwards for 30 seconds, recalls for 2 minutes and a partner marks the sheet out of 20. The class then compares the two groups' means and ranges and gives a verdict on the claim 'Believing your pen is lucky improves your memory.'
one_pager.assessment: Checkpoint out of 12 (6 questions, based on skills check question types 1 to 6), entered in the tracker (column 'W5 checkpoint') before the handover note is written. Output: trial results (group results table and worksheet Stretch). Exit ticket: placebo, control group and blind test. Logbook line: 'A fair trial needs ___ because ___.'
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
Mild deception in the memory test (about 7 minutes): explain the secret in the same lesson, straight after the test.
Taking part is voluntary: a student may watch instead; any student may withdraw their score after the debrief.
Scores are anonymous (codes only, never names); never use scores to compare individual students.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'The control group was ___ because ___.' 'The data suggests ___; however, ___.' 'To be more confident, we would need ___.' 'I think it was / was not OK because ___.' Chinese talk is welcome in the ethics debrief; report back in English with a frame. Recall may be written in English or Chinese; both count and spelling does not matter (the same rule for both groups). Checkpoint: read any question aloud in English if asked, explain everyday words, not science words; accept Chinese for Question 4. Traps: 'blind' here does not mean unable to see; 'trial' also means a court case; a placebo is a fake medicine, and the idea also applies to fake 'lucky' objects.
watch_out: Do not give the secret away before the reveal: brief the incoming teacher, treat both groups in exactly the same way and do not look at codes while students are working.
Never cut the reveal or the chance to withdraw scores. If time is short: recall 90 seconds, skip the Part B calculations and give the class means from the board, cut Challenge.

'If the lucky group scored higher, the pen works': the pens were identical, so any real difference comes from belief (placebo effect) or chance; compare a small difference in means with the ranges and the sample size.
'The placebo effect means the person is stupid or fooled': expectations affect everyone, including scientists.

one_pager.big_idea: Even a simple-sounding claim can be hard to test: scientists must agree exactly what they will measure (an operational definition), and different definitions, or different conditions, can give different answers.
goals: I can carry out a fair test of the claim 'Hot water freezes faster than cold water' (Plan A) or compare the cooling of hot and warm water (Plan B), and record my results.
I can explain what an operational definition is, show how the choice of definition can change a verdict, and say what my evidence can and cannot show.

flow.what: Three retrieval questions answered on the back of the worksheet: the control group in the lucky pen trial (Code 52), what to measure, and what 'frozen' means (write several answers on the board and keep them). Teacher checks the kit trays and, in Plan A, the freezing mixtures. Slides 1 to 2.
The Mpemba story (Tanzania, 1963; Mpemba and Osborne, 1969; a 2016 study found no clear effect; still contested). Vote: 'Do you think hot water can freeze faster?' Yes, No or Not sure. Slides 3 to 4.

one_pager.big_idea: A verdict is only as good as the data behind it, so scientists follow their plan, record raw data straight away, repeat, and note every anomaly and change honestly.
goals: I can carry out our approved plan safely and record raw data with units, repeats and notes.
I can check the quality of our data, spot anomalies and explain how we handled them.

flow.what: Trays are on the tables before students arrive; hand back the approved plans. Kit check in roles: Safety Officer ticks the tray against the plan's kit list, Lead Scientist reads the method aloud, Recorder copies the results-table headings onto the data sheet, Measurer tests the tools. 'Anything missing? Tell me now.' Slides 1 to 2.
Two data sheets for the same test, one careful and one messy: 'Which would a scientist trust? Why?' Pair talk, then one reason with a frame. Slide 3.

Three data-quality rules (2 min); anomalies and resolution (2 min); safety slide read in both languages (1 min); start signal (2 min): teacher pours warm water for claims 1, 3 and 4 in that order, claim 10 opens bottles together, ice claims take ice from the cool box, everyone starts a stopwatch on 'Go'. Slides 4 to 8, run sheet.

Groups carry out their plans in roles and record raw data in pen; teacher runs the clock from the run sheet: volunteer window opens at minute 16 and closes at minute 28; halfway check at minute 23 ('At least two repeats of each condition?'); two-minute warning at minute 30. Circulate: safety first, then consistency and recording; jot one line per student on the run sheet. Stretch on the worksheet while waiting for readings. Slides 9 to 10. If short: 2 repeats minimum; cooling claims read at 0, 5 and 10 minutes.

'Stop' at minute 32. Clean-up with the kit card (3 min); group data-quality checklist while the teacher photographs or collects every data sheet (2 min); exit ticket (2 min); logbook line 'Our first results suggest ___.' (1 min). Never cut clean-up or the checklist. Slides 11 to 12.

one_pager.practical: Each of the 6 groups carries out its own approved claim investigation from the claim bank at the same time (cooling and ice tests, people tests with volunteers, fizzy drink or paper towel tests), recording raw data in pen on a group data sheet with at least 2 repeats of each condition (3 the target).
one_pager.assessment: One data sheet per group (raw data, notes, changes), photographed or collected before students leave: the main evidence for rubric strand 3 (Doing and recording). Teacher's run-sheet notes, one line per student, support individual strand 3 levels. Exit ticket: repeats achieved, one data-quality action, one problem. Logbook line under 'What I found'.
hazards: Ice and salt mixtures are cold enough to hurt skin: gloves on; handle tubes and cups, never the mixture.
Warm water can scald: only the teacher prepares and pours it, no hotter than about 60 °C (about 50 °C for claims 3 and 4); cups and bottles stay on the tray.
No eating or drinking: nothing used in an investigation is eaten or drunk, including ice, salt and fizzy drinks.
Glass thermometers break easily: never stir with one or pull one out of ice; if one breaks, step back and tell the teacher.
Spills make floors slippery: wipe up at once.
Human participants: voluntary, no pressure, codes not names; anyone can stop or withdraw their results.
Tape measures can snap back: retract slowly and keep the metal end away from faces. Ruler drop: sit for every test.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'We noticed an anomaly in ___. We think it happened because ___. We ___ (repeated it / kept it and noted it).' 'We changed our plan because ___.' 'The data suggests ___; however, ___.' 'Would you like to take part in a short test? You can say no or stop at any time.' Chinese talk is welcome while working; readings are called out in English numbers ('thirty-four point five degrees'). Traps: 'raw' means not yet calculated, not uncooked; 'resolution' is not a New Year's resolution; 'consistent' is not 'constant'; an anomaly is an unusual result, not a mistake: it is checked, not deleted.
watch_out: 'An anomaly is a mistake, so we rub it out.' Circle it, note it, repeat if possible; never hide it.
'We changed the plan, so our results are ruined.' Sensible changes are fine if written down with a reason (rubric strand 3, Excellent).
'More decimal places means better data.' Write only what the tool can show (its resolution).
'If the result is what we predicted, the data must be good.' Good data is about method, not the answer.

one_pager.big_idea: Scientists do not just publish what they think: other scientists check their work first (peer review), and good scientists welcome criticism and change their work because of it.
goals: I can write a fact-check report that gives a verdict on the three-point scale with a confidence level, using our data as evidence.
I can review another group's report like a journal reviewer, with specific and helpful comments, and revise our own report in response to a review.

flow.what: Hand back each group's plan and data sheet (or a printed photo) with a report template; show the section-owner chart. Lead Scientist gives out sections; everyone finds the data they need. Slides 1 to 2.

How a journal decides: authors, editor, reviewers, revise, publish. 'Even Nobel Prize winners get reviewer comments.' Question: 'Why would scientists ask someone else to find problems in their work?' Slide 3.

Sample report extract (the lid report); model one reviewer comment (major issue) with the frame; major versus minor and the Low, Medium, High confidence scale. Pairs find two more problems (worksheet Core 1). Slides 4 to 5.

Groups write the report in parallel, one section each. Teacher pushes for numbers in evidence, units, the right graph type and honest limitations. At minute 18 (last 3 minutes of the draft) groups agree the verdict and confidence together. Slides 6 to 7.
Swap reports: Group 1 and 4, 2 and 5, 3 and 6. Reviewers use the checklist, check one mean with a calculator, write 3 to 5 comment slips (at least one strength) and choose a recommendation. Slide 8.

Reports returned with reviews: reply, fix major issues, fill in the revision log (5 min). Self-assessment slip (4 min). Week 10 talk frame, talk parts and exit ticket (2 min). Collect every report, revision log and reviewer checklist. Slides 9 to 11.

one_pager.practical: No practical. Each group drafts a four-page fact-check report from its Week 8 data (one section per role), reviews its partner group's report with the reviewer checklist and comment slips, then replies to the comments and revises its own report.
one_pager.assessment: A revised fact-check report per group with the reviewer checklist, comment slips and revision log attached, all collected: evidence for rubric strands 1 to 5 (judged per student before Week 10, with the plan, data sheet, logbook and Week 8 run sheet notes). Checklists and comment slips support strand 5, including for the reviewers. Self-assessment slips (do not change levels). Exit ticket: one change made, verdict with confidence, Week 10 talk part.
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
Feedback can feel personal: comment on the science, never on the people or their English.
one_pager.language_note: Frames for authors: 'We tested ___ by ___.' 'The mean ___ was ___ compared with ___.' 'Our verdict is ___ with ___ confidence because ___.' 'To be more confident, we would need ___.' Frames for reviewers: 'In section ___, ___. This matters because ___. We suggest ___.' 'The strongest part of this report is ___ because ___.' Chinese talk is welcome while drafting and reviewing; reports are written in English with key words in English; comments may be written in Chinese if needed, with key science words in English. Traps: 'review' is checking someone's work, not revising for a test; 'revise' means improve the work, not study; 'confidence' is about the evidence, not feeling brave; 'major' and 'minor' are about the effect on the verdict, not the length of the comment.
watch_out: The lesson is tight: keep strictly to the slide clock. Groups not finished drafting at minute 21 still swap, and reviewers comment on what is there ('Section 5 is missing' is a fair major comment).
Misconceptions: 'a good review only says nice things'; 'if reviewers find problems, our project failed'; 'Not enough evidence yet is a weak verdict'; 'high confidence means we did a lot of work'.
If time is short the draft and review are fixed: minimum 2 comment slips, revise major issues only, and the self-assessment slip can be skipped (it does not change levels).

one_pager.big_idea: Scientists share their verdicts in public, say honestly how sure they are, and answer questions with evidence; and after ten weeks we can see how much our own thinking has grown.
goals: I can present our claim, test, data and verdict clearly in a 2-minute talk, with a confidence level and its reason.
I can answer or ask a question from the floor using evidence, not opinion.

flow.what: Skills check papers (fresh copies of the Week 1 paper) are face down on every desk. Students sit, write name, class and date, tick 'Week 10' and do not turn over. Slide 1.

Teacher reads the instructions aloud, keeps time, gives a 5-minute warning and collects the papers at once into a labelled envelope; same rules as Week 1 (assessment/Skills_Check_Y9.md Section 0). Students work alone and in silence. Slide 2.

Teacher becomes the chair: welcomes the 'delegates', returns each group's report, gives out question cards, feedback slips and listener sheets, explains the rules and running order. Each student checks their talk part and which group they ask and give feedback to. Slides 3 to 4.

Groups 1 to 6 present standing at their own table, holding up the report graph: 2 minutes each (bell at 1 minute 45 seconds, stop at 2 minutes), then one question from the floor (about 30 seconds) from the group before. Listeners tick each verdict and confidence. Teacher records strand 6 on the marking grid. Slides 5 to 7. If short: 90 seconds and no question for the last groups.
Students finish one two stars and a wish slip for the assigned group and hand it over, while the teacher collects the verdicts onto the verdict wall poster. Slide 8.

flow.phase: Interest survey and certificates (Think and Reflect)
flow.what: Teacher reads the survey statements aloud (3 min), then presents certificates and closes the series (2 min). Slides 9 to 10. The survey is fixed; certificates can move to the next session or an assembly.

one_pager.practical: No practical. Each group gives a 2-minute talk from its table using the talk frame and its fact-check report graph (claim, test, data, verdict with confidence, limits), then answers one question from the floor. Groups show graphs and photos, not practical kit.
one_pager.assessment: Final skills check (same paper as Week 1, 20 marks) into tracker column S, growth in column T; interest survey into columns U to Z; rubric strand 6 (Communicating) from the conference marking grid, strands 1 to 5 from the report and supporting evidence, all six into columns AC to AH; awards and certificates from assessment/Rubric_and_Reporting.md Section 3. Feedback slips are not marked but can support strand 5. No exit ticket or logbook line is required.
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
Groups show graphs and photos, not practical kit: no ice, warm water or fizzy drinks at the conference.
Questions and feedback are about the science, never the people or their English.
one_pager.language_note: Talk frame on every table and on slide 5; students may hold it and read from it. The rubric judges the clarity of the science, not the English. Answer frames: 'Good question. Our data shows ___.' 'We did not test that, but we think ___ because ___.' 'That could also be explained by ___.' 'To find out, we would need ___.' Chinese is welcome while groups prepare in the opening and on feedback slips; talks and questions are in English with key words, and a stuck student may say one sentence in Chinese and then the key word in English. Skills check: the teacher may read a question aloud and explain everyday words, but not science words; Chinese answers are accepted for explanations. Traps: a 'conference' is not a lesson; 'the floor' means the audience, not the ground; 'confidence' means how strong the evidence is, not how confident the speaker feels.
watch_out: Keep the skills check first and strictly timed (15 minutes) and the survey fixed (3 minutes): they measure growth. Do not go through the answers in this lesson.
Talks run late if groups change over slowly: groups present from their own tables and the next group stands as soon as the bell goes.

'Not enough evidence yet means our project failed': say in the opening that it is an honest and respected verdict. A question from the floor is not an attack, and confidence is not the same as the verdict ('Supported, low confidence' is possible).
Award levels need strand 6 from today's talk: have both possible certificates ready for boundary students. Most Improved Scientist waits until the skills checks are marked.
